questions.stem:
The value of a car is modelled by the formula
$V=16000\mathrm{e}^{-kt}+A, \quad t\geqslant 0, t\in\mathbb{R}$
where $V$ is the value of the car in pounds, $t$ is the age of the car in years, and $k$ and $A$ are positive constants.
Given that the value of the car is £17500 when new and £13500 two years later,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) find the value of $A$,
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: Sight of $A=1500$.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) show that $k=\ln\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Substitutes $t=2, V=13500\Rightarrow 13500=16000\mathrm{e}^{-2k}+\text{'their } 1500\text{'}$ and proceeds to $P\mathrm{e}^{-2k}=...$ or $Q\mathrm{e}^{2k}=...$. Condone slips, for example, $V$ may be $1350$. It is for an attempt to make $\mathrm{e}^{\pm 2k}$ the subject. A1: $\mathrm{e}^{-2k}=\frac{3}{4}$, $0.75$ oe. dM1: For taking ln's and proceeding to $k=...$. For example $k=-\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{3}{4}$ oe. May be implied by the correct decimal answer awrt $0.144$. This mark cannot be awarded from impossible to solve equations, that is ones of the type $\mathrm{e}^{\pm 2k}=c, c\leqslant 0$. A1*: cso $k=\ln\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$ (brackets not required) with a correct intermediate line of either $\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{4}{3}$, $\frac{1}{2}\ln 4-\frac{1}{2}\ln 3$, $\ln\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}$ or $\ln\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. A1: $\Rightarrow \ln 1600-2k=\ln 1200$. dM A1*: $k=-\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1200}{1600}=\ln\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}=\ln\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$.
